statement: Seven people, including Ana and Ben, sit at a round table with seven equally spaced seats. Ana and Ben must sit next to each other. Two seatings count as the same if one is a rotation of the other. How many different seatings are there?

choices.misconception: I glued Ana and Ben into one block and used (6 - 1)! = 120, forgetting that Ben can be on either side of Ana.
I subtracted the 240 seatings with Ana and Ben together from 720, which counts the seatings where they are apart.
I used (7 - 1)! = 720 for a round table and ignored the rule that Ana and Ben sit next to each other.
I glued Ana and Ben into a block and ordered the 6 units as if in a row, 6! x 2 = 1440, forgetting that rotations are the same seating.

hints: Rotations do not matter, so you may fix where Ana sits.
Once Ana's seat is fixed, rotations are used up. Ben must take one of the two seats beside her, and the others fill the remaining seats in any order.
Fix Ana. Ben has $2$ choices of seat. The other $5$ people fill $5$ seats in $5!$ ways.

solutions.reliable: Because rotations count as the same, rotate any seating so that Ana is in one particular seat; after that, different arrangements really are different. Ben must sit in one of the $2$ seats next to Ana. The remaining $5$ people fill the remaining $5$ seats in $5! = 120$ ways. So there are $2 \cdot 120 = 240$ seatings. Transferable idea: in a circular count, pin one person to remove the rotations, then count as if in a row.
solutions.elegant: Glue Ana and Ben into one block. The block and the other $5$ people are $6$ units around a circle, in $(6 - 1)! = 120$ ways up to rotation, and the block has $2$ internal orders: $2 \cdot 120 = 240$.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
